questions.q: A strong discursive essay
o: answers the exact question with a clear, sustained line of argument
lists everything known about the topic
questions.why: Relevance and a sustained argument earn the top marks.

questions.q: Counter-arguments should be
o: raised and then evaluated or rebutted
given as much support as your own view without judgement
questions.why: Evaluation shows balance and judgement.

questions.q: A good conclusion
o: reaches a justified judgement on the question
repeats the introduction word for word
questions.why: It should follow from the argument.

questions.q: Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph in an essay on whether tourism benefits developing countries?
o: Tourism can bring vital foreign income, but its benefits are often unevenly shared.
I went on holiday to Thailand last year.
There are many things to say about tourism.
questions.why: It makes a clear, arguable point that links to the question and sets up a balanced discussion. The others are vague, anecdotal or say nothing.

questions.q: An essay question asks: 'Is censorship ever justified?' Which approach best addresses the word 'ever'?
o: Describing the history of the printing press
Listing countries that censor the media
Arguing that all censorship is bad, without examining any cases
Testing whether specific cases, such as protecting children or public safety, could justify it
questions.why: 'Ever' asks whether there is any situation at all in which it is justified, so the essay must test particular cases rather than make a blanket claim or describe background.

long.q: 'Social media does more harm than good to young people.' How far do you agree? (Plan and write in 75 minutes; mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear position that answers 'how far', stated early
B1: at least three developed arguments, each with specific evidence
B1: counter-arguments raised and evaluated
B1: a logical structure with linked paragraphs
B1: a reasoned conclusion that follows from the argument
B1: accurate, fluent and varied language

long.q: Write the introduction (about 150 words) for an essay answering: 'Is it ever right to break the law?' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: engages directly with the key terms 'ever', 'right' and 'law' (e.g. legal and moral rightness are not the same)
B1: defines or narrows the scope, e.g. peaceful protest against unjust laws versus crime for personal gain
B1: a clear, nuanced thesis that answers the question
B1: signposts the line of argument the essay will follow
B1: concise, with no empty generalisations such as 'Since the dawn of time'

long.q: Write one developed body paragraph (about 200 words) for an essay answering: 'Should the voting age be lowered to 16?' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a topic sentence that makes a clear point answering the question
B1: specific evidence, e.g. Austria lowered its national voting age to 16 in 2007; Scotland allows 16-year-olds to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections
B1: explanation linking the evidence to the claim, not just stating it
B1: a counterpoint anticipated and answered within the paragraph
B1: a closing sentence that links back to the question or on to the next point

long.q: 'Individuals, not governments, should be responsible for their own health.' To what extent do you agree? (Plan and write in 75 minutes; mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear position on 'to what extent', stated early
B1: the case for individual responsibility developed, e.g. diet, exercise, smoking as personal choices
B1: the case for government responsibility developed, e.g. poverty, food environments, sugar taxes, public healthcare
B1: specific examples from more than one country
B1: a balanced judgement that follows from the argument
B1: a logical structure with accurate, fluent and varied language

long.q: In about 10 minutes, plan an answer to: 'Is modern life too fast?' Your plan should include a thesis, at least four paragraph points (including a counter-argument), the evidence each will use, and how you will conclude. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a thesis that answers the question with some nuance (e.g. too fast for some groups or areas of life, not all)
B1: at least four distinct points in a logical order
B1: a counter-argument planned with a rebuttal
B1: specific evidence assigned to each point, not left vague
B1: a conclusion planned that follows from the points

topics.name: Economic, historical, moral, political and social topics

questions.q: Which is the best evidence to support a claim in a GP essay?
o: a specific, relevant example with context
questions.why: Precise examples make arguments convincing.

questions.q: An essay asks if a country should help poorer nations. What keeps it relevant?
o: Discussing the country-level argument the question asks about
Writing about rich individuals giving to charity
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some focused on rich individuals instead of the country context.

questions.q: How should you choose an essay question?
o: Pick the topic you know most facts about
By how well you can answer that question, not just how much you know about the topic
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many chose familiar topics they couldn't answer well.

questions.q: In an essay on whether economic growth should be a government's main aim, which use of evidence is most effective?
o: A list of growth figures for ten countries with no comment
A personal opinion that money does not buy happiness
A specific case where rapid growth came with rising inequality, explained and linked to the question
questions.why: Evidence earns credit when it is specific and its relevance to the argument is explained. Unexplained data, bare opinion and definitions do not advance the argument.

questions.q: Why should a GP essay draw examples from more than one country or region?
o: It shows a wider range of knowledge and avoids over-generalising from a single case
Examiners count the number of countries mentioned
Examples from your own country are not allowed
questions.why: A range of examples supports more convincing, qualified conclusions. Local examples are welcome, but relying on only one context invites sweeping generalisation.

long.q: 'A universal basic income is a realistic solution to poverty.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines universal basic income (a regular, unconditional payment to every citizen) and what 'solution' and 'realistic' would mean
B1: arguments for: simplicity, an end to welfare traps and stigma, security as automation changes work
B1: evidence, e.g. Finland's 2017–18 trial improved wellbeing but had little effect on employment
B1: arguments against: the cost and tax needed, possible effects on work incentives and prices, payments to the rich
B1: evaluates 'realistic', e.g. depends on a country's wealth and tax base; targeted schemes as an alternative
B1: a reasoned conclusion in accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Studying history is of little use in solving today's problems.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: interprets 'little use' and 'today's problems'
B1: for usefulness: lessons from the past, e.g. policymakers' responses to the 2008 financial crisis drew on the Great Depression
B1: for usefulness: understanding the roots of present conflicts, borders and identities
B1: against: some problems have no precedent (climate change, artificial intelligence), and history can be read selectively to justify bias
B1: a balanced judgement that answers 'how far'
B1: logical structure and accurate, varied expression

long.q: 'Wealthy nations should accept far more responsibility for refugees.' Discuss. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines who refugees are (people fleeing persecution or conflict) and what 'responsibility' could mean
B1: arguments for: moral duty, greater capacity, involvement in some conflicts, labour needs of ageing populations
B1: evidence: most refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries neighbouring the crisis
B1: arguments against or complications: pressure on services, integration, political backlash; funding host regions instead
B1: a judgement, e.g. responsibility should be shared but may take different forms (resettlement, funding)
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Older people are not valued enough in today's society.' How far do you agree, with reference to your own society? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines 'valued' (economically, socially, culturally) and refers to a specific society
B1: evidence they are valued: pensions, healthcare, multigenerational households, traditions of respect
B1: evidence they are undervalued: ageism at work, loneliness, underfunded care, digital exclusion
B1: the contribution of older people discussed: childcare, volunteering, experience
B1: a judgement that recognises variation by class, culture or circumstance
B1: logical structure and accurate, varied language

long.q: 'Democracy is the best form of government.' To what extent do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines democracy (free elections, rule of law, rights) and sets criteria for 'best'
B1: arguments for: accountability, protection of rights, peaceful transfer of power
B1: arguments against: short-termism, populism, majorities overriding minorities, slow decisions
B1: the counter-claim that some non-democratic states have achieved rapid growth, evaluated
B1: a judgement that depends on the criteria, noting that the quality of democracies varies
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

questions.q: An essay on whether technology isolates people should
o: weigh different kinds of technology and contexts
questions.why: Qualified, nuanced judgements score well.

questions.q: Which shows a balanced argument?
o: Weighing evidence on both sides and reaching a reasoned judgement
questions.why: Measured, supported points do better than sweeping claims.

questions.q: Why avoid sweeping generalisations like 'everyone has a mobile'?
o: They are inaccurate and weaken the argument
questions.why: Examiners (2023): unsupported generalisations were common.

questions.q: An essay asks: 'Should scientific research be limited by ethical concerns?' Which point shows the most nuanced thinking?
o: Ethics always matter more than science.
Limits may be justified where research risks serious harm, but blanket restrictions could delay valuable discoveries.
questions.why: It weighs both sides and sets out the conditions under which the claim holds. The first two are absolute statements and the last is irrelevant.

questions.q: Which sentence uses appropriately cautious (hedged) language?
o: Electric cars will definitely solve climate change.
Electric cars could reduce emissions, although much depends on how the electricity is generated.
Everyone agrees that electric cars are the future.
questions.why: Hedging ('could', 'much depends on') makes a claim no stronger than the evidence allows. The others overstate the case or claim universal agreement.

long.q: Evaluate the claim that governments, not individuals, should take the lead in tackling climate change. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines the scope (which governments, which individuals)
B1: argues the case for government action with examples
B1: argues the case for individual action with examples
B1: weighs the two and reaches a judgement
B1: clear structure and accurate expression

long.q: 'Space exploration is a waste of money while problems remain on Earth.' Discuss. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: interprets 'waste' and 'problems on Earth'
B1: for: high costs and the opportunity cost for health or poverty; private space tourism for the wealthy
B1: against: technology that helps people on Earth, e.g. satellites for weather forecasting, navigation and climate monitoring
B1: against: inspires interest in science, encourages international cooperation (e.g. the International Space Station)
B1: evaluates scale, e.g. space agencies receive a small share of most national budgets
B1: a reasoned judgement in accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Artificial intelligence will create more problems than it solves.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines artificial intelligence and the range of 'problems' (economic, ethical, social)
B1: problems solved: medical diagnosis, scientific research, accessibility tools, efficiency
B1: problems created: job displacement, bias in automated decisions, misinformation and deepfakes, privacy
B1: evaluates whether the problems come from the technology or from how it is regulated and used
B1: hedged, cautious claims about the future rather than certainties
B1: a reasoned judgement with a logical structure and accurate language

long.q: 'Nuclear power is the answer to the world's energy problems.' Discuss. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines 'energy problems' (security of supply, prices, emissions) and what an 'answer' requires
B1: for: low-carbon, reliable output regardless of weather, small land footprint
B1: against: high costs and long build times, long-term waste storage, accident risk (e.g. Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011)
B1: alternatives: falling costs of renewables and storage, energy efficiency
B1: a balanced judgement, e.g. part of a mix rather than 'the' answer
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Animals should never be used in medical research.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: engages with 'never' and defines medical research
B1: for using animals: medical advances (e.g. early insulin research), safety testing required before human trials
B1: against: animal suffering and rights arguments; biological differences limit how well results apply to humans
B1: alternatives: the '3Rs' (replace, reduce, refine), cell cultures, computer modelling
B1: a judgement, e.g. only where no alternative exists and under strict regulation
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

topics.name: Literature, language, the arts and media

questions.q: 'To what extent' questions require
o: a judgement on how far you agree
questions.why: They ask for degree, not just a side.

questions.q: Which is more suitable in a formal essay?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): avoid contractions and informal words.

questions.q: What is the best way to use advanced vocabulary?
o: Only where it is precise and correctly used
questions.why: Examiners (2023): complex words were sometimes used wrongly.

questions.q: An essay asks: 'Should governments fund the arts?' Which counter-argument is most relevant?
o: Public money may be better spent on essential services such as health care.
questions.why: A counter-argument must challenge the case for funding directly. The opportunity cost of public money does that, while the other statements do not bear on the question.

questions.q: Which sentence best avoids an unsupported assertion?
o: As free online news has spread, many newspapers have lost income, and some have cut back on investigative reporting.
questions.why: It explains a cause-and-effect chain and qualifies the claim with 'many' and 'some'. The others are sweeping generalisations with no reasoning.

long.q: 'Reading fiction is a waste of time in a busy world.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: interprets 'waste of time' and 'busy world'
B1: value of fiction: empathy, imagination, understanding other cultures and lives
B1: further value: language skills, concentration, rest from screens
B1: the counter-view: limited time, the appeal of non-fiction or practical learning, other forms of storytelling (film, games)
B1: a reasoned judgement that answers 'how far'
B1: logical structure and accurate, varied language

long.q: 'The news media cannot be trusted.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: distinguishes types of news media (public broadcasters, commercial outlets, online and social media)
B1: reasons for distrust: ownership and political bias, sensationalism, commercial pressure, errors
B1: reasons for trust: professional standards, regulation, fact-checking, investigative journalism
B1: the effect of social media: misinformation spreads quickly, but citizen journalism adds coverage
B1: a judgement, e.g. trust should depend on the source and on checking claims
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'There is little point in trying to preserve minority languages.' Discuss. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: explains why languages become endangered (dominant national or global languages, migration, schooling)
B1: case for preservation: identity, culture, knowledge and oral traditions carried by a language
B1: examples of revival, e.g. Welsh or Māori through schools and broadcasting
B1: the counter-view: cost, limited usefulness, people's freedom to choose a more widely spoken language
B1: a judgement that addresses 'little point'
B1: logical structure and accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Celebrities have too much influence on young people.' How far do you agree? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines 'celebrities' (including online influencers) and 'too much'
B1: negative influence: body image, consumerism, risky behaviour, unrealistic lifestyles
B1: positive influence: campaigns for good causes, role models of hard work, raising awareness
B1: the counter-view that families, peers and schools are stronger influences and young people are critical viewers
B1: a reasoned judgement in accurate, fluent language

long.q: 'Museums should return objects to their countries of origin.' Discuss. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: explains how many objects were acquired (colonial conquest, unequal purchases) and the idea of restitution
B1: case for return: justice, cultural identity, access for the communities they came from; e.g. Germany's return of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria in 2022
B1: case against or complications: legal ownership, conservation, global access in major museums, disputed origins
B1: alternatives evaluated, e.g. long-term loans, shared ownership, digital copies
B1: a reasoned judgement in accurate, fluent language

questions.q: 'Explain in your own words' means
o: paraphrase the meaning without lifting key words
questions.why: Lifting shows no understanding.

questions.q: When asked to answer in your own words, you should:
o: Rephrase without reusing the key words of the text
questions.why: Examiners (2023): reusing the original words lost credit.

questions.q: A question asks about disadvantages for one person. What loses marks?
o: Writing about advantages or about other people
questions.why: Answer exactly the angle the question sets.

questions.q: Read: 'The town's new bridge, though admired by visitors, has done little for residents, whose daily commute is now longer because the old ferry was withdrawn.' Why are residents unhappy?
o: Their journey to work takes longer now the ferry has stopped
The bridge cost too much to build
questions.why: The passage links residents' dissatisfaction to the longer commute after the ferry was withdrawn. Visitors in fact admire the bridge, and cost is not mentioned.

questions.q: Read: 'Her optimism, it must be said, was not shared by the committee.' What does this suggest?
o: The committee was more doubtful than she was
The committee agreed with her completely
She was pessimistic about the plan
The committee had not heard her views
questions.why: If her optimism was 'not shared', the committee was less hopeful or more sceptical. Nothing suggests they had not heard her.

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'The modern office worker is rarely idle and seldom productive. Meetings breed further meetings; emails beget replies to replies. We have confused motion with progress, mistaking the full calendar for the full life. Yet the remedy is not simply to work less. It is to protect long, uninterrupted stretches in which difficult thinking can happen – the kind of thinking that no meeting has ever produced.' (a) Explain in your own words what the writer means by 'rarely idle and seldom productive'. [2] (b) What does the writer mean by 'confused motion with progress'? [2] (c) Why does the writer say the remedy 'is not simply to work less'? [2] (d) Give the meaning of 'beget' as used in the passage. [1]
scheme: B1: (a) office workers are always busy or occupied
B1: (a) but they rarely achieve anything worthwhile
B1: (b) we believe that being active or busy means we are achieving something
B1: (b) when in fact activity does not necessarily produce results
B1: (c) the problem is how time is used, not how much of it is spent working
B1: (c) what is needed is uninterrupted time for deep, difficult thinking
B1: (d) produce / give rise to / generate

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'The mayor's announcement was greeted with muted applause. Her predecessor had made lavish promises and delivered little, so residents were understandably wary. The new plan was modest by comparison: repair the roads, extend the library's hours, and publish every contract online. Critics called it unambitious; supporters called it refreshingly candid.' (a) Give the meaning of each word as it is used in the passage: (i) muted (ii) predecessor (iii) lavish (iv) wary (v) candid. [5] (b) Why were residents 'understandably wary'? [1]
scheme: B1: (i) quiet / restrained / subdued
B1: (ii) the person who held the post before her
B1: (iii) extravagant / excessively generous
B1: (iv) cautious / suspicious
B1: (v) honest / frank
B1: (b) the previous mayor had made big promises but delivered little
long.ans: quiet; the previous holder of the post; extravagant; cautious; honest

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'Grandfather never threw anything away. The shed behind his house held forty years of jam jars, each one washed and labelled with whatever it contained: screws, seeds, buttons, string. When we cleared it after his funeral, my mother lingered over a jar marked simply “Useful”. It was empty. She laughed for the first time in a week, then put it, carefully, in her handbag.' (a) What impression of the grandfather does the writer create in the first two sentences? [2] (b) Why do you think the mother laughed at the jar marked 'Useful'? [2] (c) Explain the significance of the word 'carefully' in the final sentence. [2]
scheme: B1: (a) thrifty: he wasted nothing
B1: (a) orderly and methodical: every jar washed and labelled
B1: (b) the empty jar labelled 'Useful' is funny and typical of his eccentric habits
B1: (b) it brings back a fond memory of him and briefly releases her grief
B1: (c) she treats the empty jar as precious: a keepsake of her father
B1: (c) it shows her tenderness: its value is emotional, not practical

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'Supporters of four-day working weeks often cite trials in which output held steady while staff wellbeing improved. Such findings are encouraging but should be treated with caution. Firms that volunteer for trials are, almost by definition, those most likely to succeed; a hospital ward or a primary school cannot simply close on Fridays. The question is not whether a four-day week can work, but where.' (a) Explain in your own words why the writer thinks the trial results 'should be treated with caution'. [2] (b) Why does the writer mention 'a hospital ward or a primary school'? [2] (c) Explain what the writer means by the final sentence. [2]
scheme: B1: (a) the firms chose to take part themselves
B1: (a) so they are not typical: they are the ones best suited or most motivated to make it work
B1: (b) as examples of services that must run every day
B1: (b) to show that a four-day week cannot apply to every workplace
B1: (c) it is already accepted that a four-day week works in some places
B1: (c) the real task is to identify which kinds of work it suits

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'For centuries, mapmakers filled the blank spaces on their maps with sea monsters and imaginary islands. Today, satellites have photographed every part of the planet's surface, and it is tempting to think there is nothing left to discover. That would be a mistake. The deep ocean floor is mapped in less detail than the surface of Mars, and scientists estimate that most species on Earth have yet to be described.' (a) What did early mapmakers do with areas they knew nothing about? [1] (b) Explain in your own words why it is 'tempting to think there is nothing left to discover'. [2] (c) Give two pieces of evidence the writer uses to show this view 'would be a mistake'. [2] (d) How does the writer's tone change in the third sentence? [1]
scheme: B1: (a) filled them with invented things (sea monsters, imaginary islands)
B1: (b) images of the whole Earth's surface now exist
B1: (b) so it seems that everything has already been seen or found
B1: (c) the deep ocean floor is mapped less precisely than Mars
B1: (c) most species have not yet been described or identified
B1: (d) from reflective, even conceding, to firm and corrective: the short sentence asserts the writer's view

questions.q: When evaluating a source's reliability, consider
o: its author, purpose, evidence and date
questions.why: These affect how far it can be trusted.

questions.q: A correlation in data shows
o: that two things vary together, not necessarily cause and effect
proof that one causes the other
questions.why: Correlation is not causation.

questions.q: What turns a point into a developed point?
o: Explaining its likely impact or consequence
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some developments just restated the evidence.

questions.q: A survey of 20 people at a gym found that 90% exercise daily. A writer concludes that 90% of the population exercises daily. What is the main weakness?
o: The sample is small and unrepresentative of the population
The survey should have asked more questions
questions.why: Twenty gym users are a tiny sample, and a biased one, since people at a gym are more likely to exercise. The data cannot be generalised to everyone.

questions.q: A passage argues: 'Either we ban all cars from the city, or pollution will destroy it.' What is the flaw?
o: A false dichotomy, presenting only two options when others exist
questions.why: It ignores middle options such as low-emission zones or better public transport. Recognising a false choice like this is a key evaluation skill.

long.q: A passage claims a new school timetable 'improved results' because exam averages rose the following year. Identify two weaknesses in this reasoning.
scheme: B1: correlation is not causation: other factors may have changed
B1: one year's data is too little to show a trend
B1: a different cohort sat the exams, so results aren't directly comparable
B1: no information on how big the rise was or whether it is significant

long.q: A town must choose a site for a new swimming pool. Site A is in the town centre, 0.5 km from the bus station; the land costs $2 million and there is parking for 40 cars. Site B is on the edge of town, 4 km from the centre; the land costs $0.8 million, there is parking for 200 cars, and it is next to two secondary schools. A survey found that 65% of residents who say they would use the pool do not own a car. Evaluate which site is the better choice, using the information.
scheme: B1: Site A: central and near the bus station, so accessible to the many likely users without cars
B1: Site A drawback: land costs $1.2 million more and parking is limited
B1: Site B: cheaper land and much more parking
B1: Site B: next to two schools, so likely regular daytime use for lessons
B1: uses the 65% figure, e.g. Site B's parking matters less if most users don't drive, unless a bus link is added
B1: a reasoned choice, noting missing information (running costs, bus services to Site B, population distribution)

long.q: A report claims: 'Students who eat breakfast score 12% higher in tests.' The study involved 50 volunteers at one private school. Explain three reasons why this conclusion should be treated with caution.
scheme: B1: a small sample (50 students)
B1: explained: the result may be due to chance and may not be representative
B1: one private school and self-selected volunteers
B1: explained: the results cannot be generalised to students from other backgrounds or schools
B1: correlation is not causation
B1: explained: other factors, such as sleep, family income or a stable home routine, could explain both breakfast and higher scores

long.q: Read this argument. 'Ever since the new mayor took office, crime has risen. Clearly she is soft on criminals. Besides, everyone I know says they feel less safe. If we don't elect a tougher mayor next year, the city will become lawless.' Identify and explain three flaws in this reasoning.
scheme: B1: a false assumption of cause ('post hoc'): crime rising after she took office
B1: explained: the timing does not prove she caused it; other factors (the economy, changes in recording) may be responsible
B1: anecdotal evidence: 'everyone I know'
B1: explained: an unrepresentative sample, and feeling unsafe is not the same as measured crime
B1: a slippery slope or false dilemma: 'the city will become lawless'
B1: explained: an extreme outcome is predicted with no evidence and other options are ignored

long.q: A sports-drink company's website states: 'Studies show our drink improves performance by 20%.' No study is named. Assess the reliability of this claim.
scheme: B1: vested interest: the company profits if people believe the claim
B1: no named study, so the method, sample and peer review cannot be checked
B1: '20%' is vague: performance in what, measured how, compared with what (water? nothing?)
B1: what would make it more reliable: independent, peer-reviewed research with a large sample and declared funding

questions.q: Which is grammatically correct?
o: Neither the teacher nor the students were late.
Neither the teacher or the students was late.
Neither the teacher nor the students was late, and.
Neither of the teacher nor students were late.
questions.why: Neither…nor; the verb agrees with the nearer subject (students → were).

questions.q: In a summary, what should you avoid?
o: Copying long phrases and adding your own opinions
questions.why: Precision matters: choose words that keep the original meaning.

questions.q: Why must synonyms be chosen carefully?
o: A near-synonym can change the meaning
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'easily' was a poor substitute for 'contactlessly'.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The students who had revised thoroughly, found the exam straightforward.
The students, who had revised thoroughly, found the exam straightforward.
The students, who had revised thoroughly found the exam straightforward.
The students who, had revised thoroughly found the exam straightforward.
questions.why: A non-defining relative clause needs a comma at both ends. The other versions split the subject from its verb with a single comma or put the comma in the wrong place.

questions.q: Which is the most concise version of: 'Due to the fact that the weather was bad, the event was cancelled at this point in time.'?
o: Because of the fact that the weather was bad, the event was cancelled.
At this point in time, the event was cancelled due to bad weather conditions.
Owing to the weather being bad, the event has been cancelled at this time.
The event was cancelled because of bad weather.
questions.why: It removes padding such as 'due to the fact that' and 'at this point in time' while keeping the meaning. Concise, accurate expression is credited in the language-use tasks.

long.q: Read the passage, then summarise the disadvantages of remote working for employees in no more than 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Remote working, once a rare privilege, is now routine for millions. Employees save hours of commuting and many say they concentrate better at home. Yet the change has costs. Without the natural break of a journey, the working day tends to stretch into the evening, and some people find it hard to switch off. Junior staff, in particular, miss the informal learning that comes from overhearing experienced colleagues. Loneliness is a growing complaint, especially among those who live alone, and some workers fear that managers who rarely see them will overlook them for promotion. Companies, meanwhile, are cutting office space to save money.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the working day gets longer
B1: it is hard to stop thinking about work
B1: junior staff lose informal learning from experienced colleagues
B1: loneliness, especially for those who live alone
B1: fear of being overlooked for promotion
B1: own words, concise, within 80 words, with no advantages or company points included

long.q: Each sentence contains one error. Rewrite it correctly. (a) The number of students have increased. (b) Neither the teacher nor the students was ready. (c) Less people attended this year. (d) Having finished the essay, the computer crashed. (e) She was disinterested in the lecture and fell asleep. (f) The committee have made it's decision.

B1: (b) Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.

long.q: Read the passage, then summarise the effects of light pollution on wildlife and people in no more than 70 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Artificial light at night is spreading faster than the population. For wildlife, the consequences are serious. Newly hatched sea turtles, which find the sea by moving towards the brightest horizon, crawl inland towards roads. Migrating birds, confused by illuminated buildings, collide with them in their millions. Insects circle street lamps until they die of exhaustion, depriving bats and birds of food. People suffer too: bright light in the evening suppresses the sleep hormone melatonin, disturbing sleep, and most city dwellers can no longer see the Milky Way.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: turtle hatchlings are misled and head inland instead of to the sea
B1: migrating birds are confused and fly into lit buildings
B1: insects die of exhaustion around lamps
B1: bats and birds lose their food supply
B1: people's sleep is disturbed
B1: city dwellers can no longer see the night sky
B1: own words, concise, within 70 words
